1:
The book turns from Abijah to his son, and the witnesses read the opening notice — the crown passing to Asa, and in his days the land quiet ten years — as at once a formula of succession and the first token of a reign God meant to bless. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the words "So Abijah slept with his fathers" stand verbatim as at 1 Kings 15:8, where the same king is called Abijam; and he traces the ten years' quiet directly to the great victory Abijah had won, a rest the chronicler will presently explain in his own words at v.6, "he had no war in those years." The phrase "the land had rest" he sets beside the like notices of the judges at Judges 3:11 and Judges 5:31, and pauses even over the king's name, which may mean "healer," like the Syriac word for a physician, or else "spices."

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch open with a survey of the older record at 1 Kings 15:9-24, where it is told how Asa reigned forty-one years, did what was right as David had done, and removed the idols his fathers had made; and though the high places were not taken away, he was devoted to the LORD his whole life. The Chronicle, they note, characterizes him by the same word — a pious king who did that which was right.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the peaceful decade the reward of a godly beginning. Asa's tranquillity, coming after the constant alarms of the two preceding reigns, rested first on his brother's arms and then on his own piety: Abijah's victory, owing under God to his courage, laid the foundation for a peace that was the fruit of Asa's reformation. Though Abijah had little religion himself, Henry says, he was instrumental to prepare the way for one who had much — for had he not quieted the land, Asa could not have reformed it, since amidst the din of arms the voice of law is unheard. And the rest itself was God's gift: if God give quietness, who then can make trouble?

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses temper the picture with realism. Adam Clarke, following Calmet, reckons the ten years not from the very first of the reign but from Asa's fifth year to his fifteenth; and John Wesley qualifies the word "quiet," explaining that there was no open war, yet private hostilities ran on between Asa's subjects and Baasha's. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott and Keil fix the text and the older record, Henry the theology of the rest, Clarke and Wesley its exact span and its limits — together framing a reign that opens, by God's gift and a brother's sword, upon a decade of peace to be spent in reformation and building.
2:
The verdict pronounced on the new king — that he did that which was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God — the witnesses take not as a bare formula but as a heading the following verses will unfold in detail. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders it literally "the good and the right," an expression defined by the acts of reformation that follow and used again of Hezekiah at 2 Chronicles 31:20; he sets it beside the parallel at 1 Kings 15:11, "Asa did the right in the eyes of the LORD, like David his father." The "altars of the strange gods" he renders "altars of the alien," the Vulgate's altaria peregrini cultus, comparing the "gods of the alien" at Genesis 35:2; and he observes that the chronicler has here expanded into detail the bare summary of 1 Kings 15:12, that Asa "took away all the idols his fathers had made."

Ellicott presses one careful distinction that guards against an apparent contradiction. The high places Asa removed were those dedicated to foreign religions; the high places devoted to the worship of Jehovah were not done away, as is clear both from 2 Chronicles 15:17 and from 1 Kings 15:14. The "images" he takes for pillars broken in pieces, dedicated to Baal and symbolising the solar rays — a species of obelisk, like the standing stones of Exodus 34:13.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fill in the same inventory. Asa removed from all the cities of Judah the altars of the high places and the chammanim — the sun-pillars, statues consecrated to Baal as the sun-god, that were erected near or upon the altars of Baal, the same objects named at 2 Chronicles 34:4 and Leviticus 26:30. In consequence the kingdom "had rest before him," that is, under his oversight, an idiom they compare with Numbers 8:22.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verdict morally: Asa attended to what the law required of the worship of God, and though, speaking morally, he was not exempt from faults, he was no idolater, but suppressed idolatry universally and drew the people to the true God. The reformed John Gill is content to pass the verse quickly, referring the reader forward to the reformation itself. The witnesses do not divide; between them they establish that the king's good report is no empty title but the sum of a real and sweeping purge of the alien altars, sun-pillars, and idols that Judah had gathered since Solomon's decline.
3:
Only the reformed voice pauses directly on this verse, but the reformation it records draws the fuller comment of the others, and together they trace the idolatry Asa now tore down to its very root. The reformed John Gill identifies the "altars of the strange gods" as the altars of a strange people — of the Zidonians, the Ammonites, and the Moabites — which had stood in the land ever since the days of Solomon, who had built them for his foreign wives. The reformation, on this reading, reaches back across three reigns to undo the compromise with which the golden age had ended; the altars Asa demolishes are the long shadow of the shrines Solomon raised on the hill before Jerusalem, as the older record tells at 1 Kings 11:7, so that the son of David sets himself to cleanse what the wisest of David's sons had defiled.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the temper of the work. As soon as Asa had power in his hands, he says, the king made it his business to destroy all those idolatrous altars and images, which were at once a great provocation to a jealous God and a great temptation to a careless, unthinking people. And Henry marks the pastor's motive beneath the reformer's zeal: Asa hoped, by destroying the idols, to reform the idolaters — he aimed at reclaiming the worshippers rather than ruining them, breaking the altar to save the man who had bowed at it.

The grammatical-historical witnesses supply the character of the objects removed. Charles Ellicott renders the phrase "altars of the alien," the Vulgate's altaria peregrini cultus; and Keil and Delitzsch add the sun-pillars, the chammanim consecrated to Baal as the sun-god, which Asa cleared from every city of Judah, the same idolatrous furniture condemned at Leviticus 26:30. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes whose altars they were and how they came to stand in Judah; Henry weighs the reformer's aim; Ellicott and Keil describe the alien altars and sun-images themselves. Between them they show that Asa's first act of piety was a bold act of demolition — the pulling down of a foreign worship that had been tolerated so long it had become part of the very landscape, and the recalling of a whole people from the gods their fathers had let in. It is a reformation that begins not with a sermon but with an axe laid to the altars, and the deeper eloquence of the scene is that the grandson of Solomon undoes, stone by stone, the idolatry of his own house.
4:
With the altars thrown down, the king turns from demolition to command, and the witnesses read the royal edict as the positive side of the reformation. The reformed John Gill explains that Asa commanded Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers — to pray to him, and to him only, and to attend his worship and service — and that he did this by a public edict, binding the nation by law to the God whose rivals he had just destroyed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the two halves together: since the priests did their part in attending God's altars, Asa obliged the people to do theirs, commanding Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers, and not the gods of the heathen, and to do the law and the commandments — that is, to observe all those divine institutions which many had utterly neglected.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the chronicler's own hand visible in the verse, both in its construction and in its favourite phrases. "To seek the LORD God of their fathers" recurs at 2 Chronicles 15:12, in the great covenant Asa's people will later swear; and "the law and the commandment" echoes the words given at Sinai in Exodus 24:12, "the tables of stone, and the law and the commandment," repeated at Deuteronomy 6:25. The "images" of the verse he again identifies as the hammanim, the sun-pillars standing before or upon the altars of Baal — kin to the Phoenician deity Baal-hamman — named also at Isaiah 17:8 and Leviticus 26:30. And the closing clause, "the kingdom was quiet before him," he glosses as a land that enjoyed peace under the king's oversight, comparing the sense of "before" at Numbers 8:22 and Psalms 72:5.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, read the command as the crown of the reforming work — to seek the LORD and to do the law and the commandment — the whole a single movement by which the king first cleared the ground of alien worship and then planted his people afresh in the covenant. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Henry weigh the substance of the edict, that a nation is summoned back to its God by royal authority; Ellicott and Keil trace the chronicler's language and its roots in the law of Moses. Between them they show that Asa's reformation was not merely negative but constructive: he did not leave the swept house empty, but bound Judah, priests and people alike, to seek the God of their fathers and to walk in his commandments.
5:
The chronicler repeats and widens the reckoning of the purge — the high places and the sun-images swept from all the cities of Judah — and the witnesses read the verse as the measure of how thorough the reformation was. The reformed John Gill distinguishes the sphere of this cleansing from the last: perhaps the earlier notice touched chiefly the high places and altars in and about Jerusalem, while here the reach extends to all the rest of the cities of the land. The "images," he says, are as the word signifies sun-images — figures made in the form of the sun, or dedicated to it, or temples raised for its worship.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather this verse with the two that follow into a single account of Asa's use of the peace. Having taken away the high places and the sun-images, so that the kingdom had rest before him, the king turned the ten years' quiet to the building of fortresses in Judah. "Let us build these cities," he said, "and make about them walls and towers, gates and bars, while the land is yet before us"; and because they had sought the LORD their God, and he had given them rest on every side, they built and prospered.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, adds the caution he had pressed before: the high places done away were those given to foreign religions, for it is plain from 2 Chronicles 15:17, as from 1 Kings 15:14, that the high places devoted to the worship of Jehovah were not removed in Asa's day — a distinction that saves the record from contradicting itself. The witnesses do not divide. Gill weighs the reach and the nature of the sun-images; Keil sets the cleansing in its place as the ground of the building that follows; Ellicott guards the exact sense of "high places." Between them they portray a king whose reforming zeal ran through every city of his realm, and whose reward was a settled quiet — the "rest before him" that he would spend not in ease but in fortifying the land against the day of trouble. The purged kingdom becomes the building kingdom; the same energy that pulled down the alien altars now raises the walls of Judah, and the chronicler binds the two together as cause and effect, cleansing and blessing, so that the reader sees the reformation flower at once into strength.
6:
The building of the fenced cities, named here for the first time, draws the witnesses to both its strategy and its theology. The reformed John Gill reads the work as defence: Asa fortified cities in Judah against the kingdom of Israel and the other nations round about, as Rehoboam his forefather had done before him, and perhaps rebuilt some that Shishak king of Egypt had thrown down when he came up against the land. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way — the fenced cities were raised to preserve the king's territories from invasion and to strengthen the frontiers of his kingdom.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the enterprise in the line of the chronicler's earlier notices, comparing the fortifications of Rehoboam at 2 Chronicles 11:5 and the fenced cities of 2 Chronicles 12:4; and the phrase "had given him rest" he traces to the great promise of rest to David at 2 Samuel 7:1. Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, gather the reason the verse itself gives: the land had rest, and Asa had no war in those years, because the LORD had given him rest — and it was precisely this God-given quiet that he employed in building his fortresses.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley lifts the note of rest into a meditation. Those have rest indeed, he says, to whom God gives rest; peace indeed, to whom Christ gives peace; and we find by experience that it is good to seek the LORD, while those who pursue the world meet with nothing but vexation. The witnesses do not divide, and their several notes compose a single picture. Gill and Clarke fix the strategy — a shrunken kingdom bracing its borders against Israel and Egypt alike; Ellicott and Keil ground the peace in the covenant rest God bestowed; Wesley draws the devotion out of it. Between them they show a king who understood that the quiet God gives is not for idleness but for labour, and who spent the years of peace making his people safe against the war he knew must one day come. And the wisdom of the work would soon be proved on the field, for the fenced cities were no idle labour: Mareshah, where Asa would presently face the vast Ethiopian host, was itself one of these fortified towns of Judah. The rest is God's gift; the walls are the wise use Asa made of it.
7:
Asa's own words to his people, quoted here, turn the building into a shared resolve, and the witnesses attend to the summons and to the reasoning behind it. The reformed John Gill notes that the king addressed himself to the nobles and the principal men of the kingdom, laying the enterprise before those whose leadership would carry it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the speech the wisdom of a ruler who prepares in peace for trouble. Asa fortified his principal cities with walls, towers, gates, and bars, urging, "This let us do while the land is yet before us" — that is, while we have the opportunity and advantage, and nothing to hinder us. He speaks, Henry says, as one who expected that some way or other trouble would arise, when it would be too late to fortify and they would wish they had; in times of peace we must be getting ready for trouble, and when the sword is sheathed take up the trowel. So they built and prospered.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings his customary care to the wording and the history. These "cities," he observes, are the fenced cities of the previous verse, and their names are not given; the fortifying of Geba and Mizpah came later, only after the war with Baasha that began in Asa's twenty-sixth year, as told at 1 Kings 15:33 and 2 Chronicles 16:6. A general system of defence, like Rehoboam's fifteen cities, seems intended here. The phrase "while the land is yet before us" he takes to mean that the land lay open to them, free from hostile occupation, an expression borrowed from Genesis 13:9; and he even proposes, dropping the word "while," to read the connection of thought as, "The land is still before us, for we have sought the LORD" — the building a fruit of the seeking. "So they built and prospered," he closes, means they built prosperously, without let or hindrance.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the audience of the speech, Henry its prudence, Ellicott its wording and its place in the chronology of the reign. Between them they show a king who does not fortify by decree alone but persuades his leaders to the work, grounding it in the God-given peace and pressing it forward while the doing is still possible — the model of a wisdom that lays up in the calm against the coming storm, and that reads its very opportunity to build as the evidence of a favour already received.
8:
The muster of Asa's army, set down in round numbers, draws the witnesses to the make-up of the force and to the great figures the chronicler records. The reformed John Gill notes that the men of Judah bore a large sort of shield to protect them and spears to push at the enemy and close to quarters, while the men of Benjamin, as the verse adds, bore shields and drew bows. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the equipment: targets perhaps furnished with a dagger in the centre and javelins for the distant fight, and the Benjamites not only archers but armed with shield and sword for close combat as well.

The grammatical-historical witnesses draw the tactical distinction more sharply. Charles Ellicott makes the men of Judah the heavy-armed — hoplites, a Greek writer would say — bearing the large shield or buckler and the lance, as at 2 Chronicles 9:15 and 1 Chronicles 12:24, and the men of Benjamin the light-armed, the peltasts, with the short round shield of 2 Chronicles 9:16 and the bow of 1 Chronicles 8:40. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same two arms, the large shield and lance of Judah, the small shield and bow of Benjamin.

On the numbers the witnesses are candid. Ellicott reckons the total at five hundred and eighty thousand — three hundred thousand of Judah and two hundred and eighty thousand of Benjamin — set beside Abijah's four hundred thousand at 2 Chronicles 13:3, and grants that the whole male population capable of bearing arms must be included, for no standing army of such strength is to be thought of; the proportion of Benjamin, he owns, appears much too high, though the tribe was always famed for its warriors, as at Genesis 49:27. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the Benjamite figure is very large, and probably founded on an overestimate. Yet both grammatical-historical voices see a deeper purpose in the reckoning: the chronicler records the great host, Keil says, only to show that Asa set his hope of victory over the innumerable Cushites not on the strength of his army but on the all-powerful help of the LORD — a trust the next scene will put to the proof. And the union of the two tribes in one array, Judah's heavy foot and Benjamin's archers standing side by side, is itself a quiet mark of the kingdom's recovered strength under a godly king. The witnesses do not divide; they weigh the arms, question the numbers, and hear beneath them the note that will govern the battle to come.
9:
The peace is broken by an invasion on a scale unmatched in the book, and the witnesses gather to identify the invader, his people, and his prodigious host. The reformed John Gill weighs the old question whether these were the Ethiopians of Africa, beyond Egypt, or the Cushite Arabs who dwelt in Midian and Arabia nearer to Judah; and though he lays out the case for the nearer people, he inclines at last to the Africans, since the host was joined by the Lubim or Libyans, and these Ethiopians had become masters of Egypt and Libya soon after the death of Shishak. From Josephus he reports the army at nine hundred thousand foot and a hundred thousand horse. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that Zerah was probably of the Ethiopia lying south of Egypt, near Libya, whose people are joined with his at 2 Chronicles 16:8; but John Wesley takes the other road, reading "Ethiopian" as "the Arabian," since the Hebrew Cush is commonly so used, and these lay much nearer to Asa.

Over the person of Zerah the grammatical-historical witnesses divide. Charles Ellicott identifies him with Osorchon II, the hieroglyphic Uasarken, who succeeded Shishak on the throne of Egypt, and reads the whole expedition as an attempt to bring Judah again under the Egyptian yoke that Shishak had laid on Rehoboam at 2 Chronicles 12:8 — Asa having restored his defences and reorganised his forces in a bid for independence. Keil and Delitzsch report the usual identification with Osorchon I, but note that Brugsch objected, holding Zerah to have been an Ethiopian and not an Egyptian prince, who marched through Egypt as a conqueror.

The "thousand thousand" itself the witnesses handle warily. Gill and, with him, the older reckoning take it for a literal army of a million; but Ellicott judges the vast and symmetrical figure best rendered by an indefinite word like "myriads," being otherwise out of all proportion to the three hundred chariots, which alone seems a sound datum. Clarke adds a soldier's doubt: had such a multitude come from any great distance, they could never have found forage. On the field they agree: Zerah came to Mareshah, one of Rehoboam's fortresses in the lowland of Judah, some twenty-six miles south-west of Jerusalem, named at 2 Chronicles 11:8. The witnesses divide over the invader's homeland and name and even the size of his host, yet converge on the peril: a peace-loving reformer, his ten years of quiet ended, must now face at his own gate the largest army Judah had ever seen.
10:
Asa does not wait behind his new walls but marches out, and the witnesses mark both the boldness of the sortie and the ground on which he met the foe. The reformed John Gill notes the courage of it — Asa went out against Zerah notwithstanding the vast army he had brought — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the phrase "before him," the king going forth to face the host rather than to be besieged by it. Both armies drew up in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah, and there the king "called upon the LORD his God for help."

The location itself the grammatical-historical witnesses cannot quite fix. Keil and Delitzsch reject the identification of Zephathah with Tel es Safieh that Robinson had proposed, judging the valley to have lain nearer Mareshah, to the west or north-west of it. Ellicott too calls the valley unidentified, and records that the Septuagint read instead "in the ravine north of Mareshah," a sense that would require the change of but a single Hebrew letter, while the Syriac and Arabic have simply "in the wady of Mareshah." The ground is uncertain, but the witnesses agree it lay hard by the fortress-town where Zerah had halted.

What holds their deeper attention is the pivot the verse turns on. Asa had mustered his five hundred and eighty thousand and gone out in battle array; yet, drawn up before an enemy who doubled and trebled his numbers, the king's last act before the clash was not a word of command but a cry to God. Keil and Delitzsch, tracing the prayer that follows, hear in it the confession that trust is placed not in the army but in the LORD — "in Thy name are we come against this multitude," and "let not a mortal retain strength with Thee," phrases they set beside 2 Chronicles 13:20 and 1 Chronicles 29:14. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott mark the boldness of the march and the disputed field; Keil sets the scene for the prayer. Between them they show a reformer who had built and armed with all diligence, yet who, at the decisive hour, laid the whole weight of the day not on his own preparations but on the God he had sought — the very lesson the chronicler had planted in the muster of the verse before. The mightiest levy in Judah's history goes into the field leaning not on its own arm but on a prayer.
11:
Asa's battlefield prayer, short but weighty, is the heart of the chapter, and the witnesses gather around its confidence and puzzle over its exact words. The reformed John Gill notes that the king cried unto the LORD with vehemence, in his distress, before the battle joined, at the head of his army and for its encouragement. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the prayer's four movements: Asa gives God the glory of his infinite power and sovereignty, that it is nothing with him to help by many or by few, as Jonathan had confessed at 1 Samuel 14:6 and the psalmist at Psalms 21:13; he lays hold of the covenant-relation, "O LORD, thou art our God"; he pleads their dependence, "we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude"; and he interests God in the cause, "let not man prevail against thee" — for if a mortal prevail against a people who go forth in God's name, it will be said that he prevails against God himself. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out that last plea in the same key: if the enemy prevail against us, he prevails as it were against thee, because thou art our God.

Over the opening clause the grammatical-historical witnesses raise a real question of translation. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, with Bertheau, render it not "it is nothing with thee to help" but "none is with thee to help between a mighty one and a weak" — that is, none but thou canst help the weaker side in an unequal battle. Charles Ellicott presses a like sense, "there is none beside thee to help between strong and powerless," and records the emendation of Kamphausen, who by reading one word differently would give, "it is not for any to retain strength with thee, whether strong or powerless," comparing 2 Chronicles 13:20. Adam Clarke keeps the received sense and adds the Targum's paraphrase, that Judah came against the host "in the name of thy Word."

The witnesses divide over the wording but not over the substance. Whether the plea is that God can save by many or few alike, or that God alone can help the weaker in an uneven fight, or that no man can withstand him at all, the confession is one: the day belongs not to the larger army but to the LORD. Ellicott notes that the very word for the enemy "multitude," hamon, is the term used of Jeroboam's host at 2 Chronicles 13:8. Between them the witnesses show a king who had prepared everything and trusted none of it, resting the whole issue on the God whose honour was now bound up with his people's cause.
12:
The answer to the prayer is immediate and total, and the witnesses mark both the divine hand that struck and the terror that scattered the vast host. The reformed John Gill reads the blow as a stroke of consternation: the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah, throwing them into a panic. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same in a word — they were smitten with terror, an unaccountable consternation. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the order of the victory carefully: first God defeated the enemy and put their forces into disorder, smiting them so that they fled and knew neither why nor whither, and only then did Asa and his soldiers take the advantage God had given them. The rout, in other words, was God's before it was Judah's; the prayer of the previous verse is answered the instant it is uttered.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the completeness of the overthrow. So many of the Cushites fell, they explain, that "to them was no revival" — they could not make a stand and gather themselves again; and they are careful to correct a looser rendering, showing that the phrase denotes not that "nothing living" was left but that the host had no means of recovery, a strong expression for utter defeat. They add that the enemy was "broken before Jahve and before his host," the army of Asa reckoned as the army of God.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, brings a note of external corroboration. He reports the observation of Thenius, that the very treasures Asa afterwards dedicated in the temple, mentioned at 1 Kings 15:15, help to establish the chronicler's account of this victory and of Abijah's before it, comparing the like triumph at 2 Chronicles 13:15. The witnesses do not divide. Gill, Wesley, and Henry weigh the panic and the divine agency behind it; Keil measures the ruin; Ellicott finds the corroborating trace in the older record. Between them they portray a battle decided not by the shock of arms but by a terror sent from heaven — the God whom Asa had sought going out before his people, so that a million could not stand against a king who trusted him. Gill marks that the stroke fell "before Asa and before Judah," the LORD himself the agent and the army but the witness of what he did; and the suddenness of it — a rout with no cause the Cushites could name — is the very shape of an answered prayer.
13:
The rout becomes a pursuit, and the witnesses follow the broken host to Gerar and weigh the strong words with which the chronicler describes their end. The reformed John Gill marks Gerar as a city of the Philistines, the goal of the chase. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the flight to the ancient Philistine town whose ruins Rowlands had found at Khirbet el Gerar, some three leagues south-south-east of Gaza, near the place named at Genesis 20:1; and they infer that the cities round Gerar, which Judah also smote, had made common cause with the Cushites, being themselves inhabited by Philistines, so that the "fear of Jahve" — the dread of the omnipotence displayed in the enemy's annihilation, as at 1 Samuel 11:7 — fell upon them all. Ellicott sets the same ruin some eight miles south-south-east of Gaza, on the road down to Egypt, the town the Septuagint names Gedor.

The strongest phrase of the verse — that the Ethiopians "could not recover themselves" — the witnesses read with a shade of difference. Keil and Delitzsch take it to mean that so many fell that no revival was possible, no rallying of the shattered force. Charles Ellicott prefers "until they had no survival," a vivid hyperbole for complete annihilation, like the corpses of 2 Kings 19:35, and matched by the Vulgate's phrase "even to extermination." Whether the sense is that none could rally or that none was left, the picture is of a host destroyed beyond recovery.

On the theology of the pursuit the witnesses are one. The fallen were "destroyed before the LORD, and before his host," and Ellicott presses the phrase home: Asa's army is the LORD's army, his camp the camp of God. Matthew Henry had drawn the same point, that the Ethiopians fell before the LORD, for who can stand before him, and before his host — whether an unseen army of angels or the host of Israel owned as God's own. Much spoil was taken. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the place and the Philistine allies; Ellicott and Keil weigh the word of ruin; Henry and Ellicott read the victory as God's. Between them they show the pursuit carrying the judgment of heaven all the way to the Philistine border, so that the terror which routed Zerah unmanned his confederates too, and Judah gathered the plunder of a field that God had won.
14:
The victory spreads outward to the towns about Gerar, and the witnesses attend to why those cities were struck and to the divine dread that made them fall. The reformed John Gill identifies them as cities of the Philistines, auxiliaries and confederates of the invaders and colonies akin to them, noting that in Theodoret's day a place near Eleutheropolis still bore a name recalling Gerar. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that these were Philistine cities hostile to Judah, which had perhaps helped Zerah, and so shared his fall.

The heart of the verse, for the witnesses, is the "fear of the LORD" that came upon those cities. Ellicott renders it "a divine panic," the same supernatural terror that fell on Israel's enemies at 1 Samuel 11:7 and again at 2 Chronicles 17:10. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it as the reason no resistance could be made: a fear which God struck the cities with, to such a degree that they had no heart to withstand the conquerors. The dread that had scattered the great army now unnerved the towns that had leagued with it, so that Judah spoiled them at will.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the practical ground of the plunder: these cities lay in the rear of the vast host and had laid up much forage for it, and to seize that store the men of Judah overthrew the whole. Ellicott adds a philologist's note on the very word for the booty, bizzah, a late term found again at Ezekiel 29:19, where the previous verse had used the older and more classical shalal. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott name the confederate cities; Henry and Ellicott weigh the God-sent panic that laid them open; Clarke explains the forage that made them worth the taking. Between them they show the completeness of the deliverance: not only the army but its allies and its supply were swept away, and the fear of the LORD did in the towns of Philistia what the sword had done in the valley of Zephathah, so that the spoil of the whole confederacy fell into the hands of the people who had trusted God. Ellicott hears in that God-sent dread the same terror that had unmanned the Philistines of old before the ark at 1 Samuel 4:7; it was no natural flight but the hand of heaven, turning even the allies of Judah's enemy into its plunder.
15:
The campaign closes with the plunder of the herdsmen's camps and the return home, and the witnesses divide mildly over just whose tents these were. The reformed John Gill takes the "tents of cattle" for the dwellings of people who lived in tents for the sake of the pasturage of their flocks — the Scenite Arabs, so called from their tents. Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, reads them likewise as the encampments of nomad Bedawin whom Judah encountered in the desert about Gerar, comparing the "tents" smitten at 1 Chronicles 4:41. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, however, takes them rather for the cattle-camps of Zerah's own host — the enclosures where the beasts that had carried the great army's baggage were left in places abounding with pasture, perhaps sheepfolds and pens for camels and mules. Whether the tents belonged to wandering herdsmen or to the invaders' baggage-train, the spoil was the same: sheep and camels in abundance.

Keil and Delitzsch simply record the close — they smote the tents of cattle, carried away sheep and camels in abundance, and returned to Jerusalem — the army coming home laden from a war it had scarcely needed to fight. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole plunder into a proverb: the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just, as it is written at Proverbs 13:22; the cattle fetched in vast numbers out of the enemy's country became the reward of a people who had gone to war in God's name.

Clarke lets the campaign end on a note of wonder and of candour. The discomfiture was great, he says, because God fought for the people, and the spoil immense because the multitude was prodigious; yet he owns that a host of a million men in one place is almost too much for the mind to conceive, and allows that there may be some mistake in the numerals, though the number was plainly vast and the spoil great. The witnesses do not, in the end, divide. Gill and Ellicott take the tents for nomad herdsmen, Clarke for the enemy's baggage-camps, but all agree on the completeness of the victory and the richness of the return. Between them they bring Asa home to Jerusalem crowned with spoil — the reformer who sought the LORD, trusted him against a million, and came back to his capital with the wealth of his enemies in his train.
